newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Analysts see SNB still favouring lower money rates.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see SNB still favouring lower money rates.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) still wants to keep upward pressure off money market rates, despite recent tightness in that market, analysts said on Wednesday.
An SNB spokesman said in response to an enquiry that SNB policy hasn't changed since the central bank cut its discount rate on September 26 to 1.00 percent from 1.50 percent.

But some currency market traders were wondering on Wednesday why the SNB had not added sufficient liquidity to the money market to keep short term rates from rising over 1-1/2 percent. Such a move would have been in keeping with the SNB's desire to keep the Swiss franc from appreciating, they said.

Michael Bernegger, currency analyst at CS, blamed technical factors for keeping money rates firm, citing banks' need for funds to meet reserve requirements before the end of the latest liquidity period on October 19.

"It seems that a few big banks, at the start of liquidity period, had expected rates would decline, but rates didn't. So they need money now, and it could be that it (the liquidity) is poorly distributed," Bernegger said.
His comments followed the Swiss franc's drop to four and a half month lows against the dollar this morning, as the U.S. unit rose to 1.2725 Swiss francs in Asia.

But Bernegger expected short term rates to ease back again to around 1-1/2 percent, and said the SNB may even consider further lowering money market rates in a month or so, if the economy continues to show significant weakness.

The SNB has been seen as working to keep money market rates low in order to discourage demand for the Swiss franc. The strength in the Swiss franc works against exports and improving exports is seen as the most likely way to lift the Swiss economy out of recession.
The SNB does not specify a target for money market rates, and dealers have seen two-day, or tomorrow/next money rise to over 1-1/2 percent from levels closer to 1-3/8 percent in late September.
Some market participants believe the SNB may wish to keep its powder dry in the event the Swiss franc strengthens again.

Hans-Peter Hausheer, economist at Swiss Bank Corp, said the SNB is probably still seeking a weaker franc but some factors, including the future shape of EU economic and monetary union, were likely to create an uncertain environment which may threaten to push the franc higher.
Uncertainty remains whether "soft-currency" countries, including Italy, will join EMU at the start in 1999.
Analysts also set store by SNB board member Bruno Gehrig's comments published in Swiss journal Finanz und Wirtschaft earlier this month.
Gehrig said the SNB's discount rate cut had not yet been fully reflected in the franc's exchange rate.

"Without doubt there is scepticism in the market about whether the SNB will continue the flexible money market policy that it started this summer. If we continue, this conviction will take hold in the market," Gehrig said.
